documents: Zhang, Li, Wang, Cheng & Tang (2023) Q estimation based on the centroid frequency and standard deviation of frequency-weighted-exponential function. Geophysical Prospecting 71, 48-62 (published PDF)

entry.evidence: Unfortunately, the constant symmetry index assumption reduces the accuracy of the FWE method when the wavelet shape is not a standard FWE wavelet.

sequences.source_document: Zhang et al. 2023, Geophysical Prospecting 71, 48-62 (published PDF)

steps.action: Reviewed frequency-domain Q estimators (LSR, PFS, CFS, FWE). Posed the problem that the FWE method's constant symmetry index assumption degrades Q accuracy for non-standard wavelet shapes.
steps.quote: Unfortunately, the constant symmetry index assumption reduces the accuracy of the FWE method when the wavelet shape is not a standard FWE wavelet.

steps.action: Named the rival remedies from other groups: recalculating an optimal symmetry index by average or least-squares methods, and the synthetic CFS (SCFS) method of Li et al. (2020).
steps.quote: Li et al. (2020) form a synthetic wavelet and replace the symmetry index with the centroid frequency and variation of this wavelet.

steps.action: Restated the theory of the CFS and FWE methods: the attenuation model (Eq. 1), the Gaussian-spectrum CFS formula (Eq. 4) and the FWE Q formula with its symmetry index (Eqs 5-7, Appendices A-B).
steps.quote: Quan and Harris (1997) design the centroid frequency shift (CFS) method under the consideration that the spectrums are a specific type like Gaussian shape.

steps.action: Propagated a Gaussian wavelet and a high-pass-filtered Gaussian wavelet through a medium with Q = 80 for 0.1-1 s. Compared the CFS and FWE estimates with the true Q (Table 1, Figure 3a-b), showing that the symmetry index is not constant.
steps.quote: In the following experiments, we exhibit the advantages and disadvantages of the CFS and FWE methods.

steps.action: Derived the IFWE formula (Eq. 12), which replaces the symmetry index with the standard deviations of the source and attenuated spectra; all parameters are computed directly from the spectra.
steps.quote: In our method, the optimal problem brought by the constant symmetry index is reduced by substituting the symmetry index with the standard deviations of the [...]

steps.action: Showed analytically that Eq. 12 reduces to the CFS formula for a Gaussian wavelet and to the FWE formula for a standard FWE wavelet. Stated that the method applies when the real spectrum fits a Gaussian, Ricker or FWE wavelet.
steps.quote: Besides, for the Gaussian wavelet, Equation (12) is the same as Equation (4).

steps.action: Tested CFS, FWE and IFWE on a standard FWE wavelet and a low-pass-filtered FWE wavelet with Q = 80 (Table 1, Figure 3c-d). IFWE had the lowest relative errors.
steps.quote: To prove the applicability of the proposed method, a simple experiment is designed as follows.

steps.action: Designed noise-free synthetic records with Gaussian, Ricker and FWE source wavelets (Figure 5), varying Q (15-135) and travel time (0.1-1 s), to compare IFWE with CFS, FWE and SCFS by relative Q error.
steps.quote: Then the relative Q errors of the three methods are calculated under different attenuation degrees.

steps.action: For the Gaussian wavelet, compared relative errors and the attenuated-spectrum standard deviation and symmetry index (Figure 6). IFWE was the most accurate and FWE the worst.
steps.quote: The IFWE method (red line) maintains low relative errors as the Q value increases.

steps.action: For the Ricker wavelet (Figure 7), SCFS was the most accurate and IFWE second, both ahead of FWE and CFS.
steps.quote: Although the IFWE method does not perform as well as the SCFS method, it takes into account the shift of the centroid frequency and the [...]

steps.action: For the FWE wavelet (Figures 8-9), CFS errors exceeded 10% in places, while SCFS and IFWE had almost the same accuracy and beat FWE.
steps.quote: which demonstrates the almost same accuracy of the two methods

steps.action: Summarized the noise-free tests: SCFS and IFWE both beat CFS and FWE. IFWE is better for Gaussian wavelets, SCFS for Ricker, and the two are similar for FWE.
steps.quote: In conclusion, the SCFS and IFWE methods reduce the impact of the symmetry index on the basis of the FWE method, and both of them [...]

steps.action: Added random noise to Ricker-wavelet records with 100 independent realizations per level. Varied the upper frequency limit from 120 to 40 Hz at SNR 12.5 dB and travel time 0.3 s (Figure 10a), then fixed it at 90 Hz.
steps.quote: For each SNR level, we conduct 100 independent experiments.

steps.action: Varied SNR from 5 to 17.5 dB and travel time from 0.3 to 0.6 s (Figure 10b-c). IFWE matched or slightly beat SCFS under noise, and was accurate above 12.5 dB SNR with a suitable upper frequency limit.
steps.quote: the IFWE method can obtain accurate and relatively stable results when the SNR is greater than 12.5 dB

steps.action: Took a 2D poststack seismic profile from an oil field (800-1600 ms, 2 ms sampling) with two horizons bounding the target zone and four wells: one productive, two oil-bearing water layers, one dry (Figure 11).
steps.quote: Figure 11 is the profile of the real seismic poststack record from an oil field.

steps.action: Extracted source spectra from eight overlapping windows above the target and attenuated spectra from 1260-1460 ms, smoothed them by quadratic spectrum simulation, and fitted Gaussian, Ricker and FWE functions. This checks the premise that the real spectra are near-FWE (Figure 12).
steps.quote: the modelled FWE function matches the wavelet spectrums better than other functions

steps.action: Estimated eight Q values per trace with CFS, FWE, SCFS and IFWE (upper frequency 80 Hz), removed high-SD results, averaged, and spline-interpolated Q curves along the profile (Figure 13).
steps.quote: Next, we can get eight Q values in each trace from the corresponding source and attenuated wavelet spectrums.

steps.action: Compared the Q curves with the well interpretations (low Q expected at oil wells, high at the dry well). All methods show low Q near wells 3-4; IFWE comes closest at wells 1 and 2.
steps.quote: The consideration of standard deviations and centroid frequencies makes the results of the IFWE method the closest to the well interpretations.

steps.action: Concluded that IFWE outperforms CFS and FWE, is better than SCFS for Gaussian wavelets and similar for FWE wavelets, is robust above 12.5 dB SNR, and is effective for fluid indication in field data.
steps.quote: Compared with the SCFS method, the IFWE method is more suitable for the Gaussian type, and the accuracy of the two is similar under the [...]

tree.answer: Q estimates from FWE are biased when the wavelet is not a standard FWE shape (symmetry index not constant)
No; Q is a latent quantity inferred from spectral shifts
Build a Q estimator free of the constant-symmetry-index assumption
Rival estimators CFS, FWE and SCFS
Methods differ in relative Q error by wavelet shape and attenuation degree on synthetics with known Q
Conditions set: synthetic wavelets, Q, travel time, SNR and upper frequency chosen by the authors
Partly: robust above 12.5 dB SNR with a suitable upper frequency limit; beaten by SCFS on noise-free Ricker records
IFWE kept as more accurate than CFS and FWE and comparable to SCFS; field Q curves consistent with wells

end.claim: The IFWE method, which replaces the FWE symmetry index with the spectral standard deviations, estimates Q more accurately than CFS and FWE across wavelet shapes. It matches or beats SCFS for Gaussian and FWE wavelets and under noise above 12.5 dB SNR, and gives field Q curves consistent with well interpretations.

decisive_move.sentence: Deriving Eq. 12, which substitutes the source and attenuated spectral standard deviations for the constant symmetry index, creates the IFWE estimator; every later test characterizes it.

gates.evidence: The synthetic records were designed to test the IFWE formula against CFS, FWE and SCFS with known true Q, and the method could have lost. It did lose to SCFS for noise-free Ricker wavelets (p. 56). The field data were existing poststack records not acquired for the hypothesis (p. 59). No preregistration; the upper-frequency limits (90 Hz synthetic, 80 Hz field) were chosen after inspecting results (pp. 57, 59).

imports.item: Fast Fourier transform for spectra of windowed traces
Butterworth high-pass and low-pass filters to make non-standard wavelets
Spectral moments (centroid frequency, variance and standard deviation of a spectrum)
Spline interpolation of trace-wise Q values

novelty_claims.quote: the basic idea of a novel Q estimation method is to substitute the symmetry index with the standard deviation
a novel formula is derived by the centroid frequency and the standard deviations
Unlike the synthetic centroid frequency shift (SCFS) method, a new formula is [...]

limits: No review file was supplied, so only the published text is coded. The real data are not public (p. 60). In the field the true Q is unknown, so the check against wells is qualitative: low Q at oil wells, high at the dry well (p. 60). The field-data sub-claim is at best best_explanation-level consistency, not a test with a known answer. The noise-robustness sub-claim is regularity_in_range (holds above 12.5 dB SNR with a suitable upper frequency limit, pp. 57-59) and was shown only for the Ricker wavelet (Figure 10). The claimed superiority over SCFS holds only for Gaussian wavelets noise-free and for Ricker wavelets under noise; SCFS was better for noise-free Ricker records (pp. 56-57). Some errors smaller than CFS are attributed to numerical error (pp. 54, 56). The text says 'three methods' where four are compared (p. 55) and cites 'Equation (9)' for the symmetry-index expressions of Eq. 7 (p. 52). Inference: the order of experiments in the text may not reflect the order in which the work was done, and the choice of upper-frequency limits looks post hoc. Composition coded none_fits: this is a method paper that starts from a named limitation of an existing estimator and characterizes a new estimator against existing rivals on synthetics with known truth, then on field data. capability_first does not fit because the rivals exist from the start, and strong_inference does not fit because no rival is excluded outright.

disagreements.support: Table 1 and Figure 3 show that the symmetry index varies with attenuation for non-FWE wavelets, giving larger Q errors than IFWE.
disagreements.quote: the constant symmetry index assumption reduces the accuracy of the FWE method when the wavelet shape is not a standard FWE wavelet

disagreements.target: Recalculated optimal symmetry index methods (Jiang et al., 2018; Li & Liu, 2015, 2016; Li et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2018)
disagreements.support: Asserted without a direct test of those specific schemes; the authors argue that a constant index cannot be made optimal.
disagreements.quote: Even so, the obtained symmetry indexes are [...] .

disagreements.support: Synthetic tests with filtered Gaussian, Ricker and FWE wavelets show large CFS errors when the spectrum is asymmetric (Figures 3, 7, 8).
disagreements.quote: which makes it unsuitable for the other wavelet shapes

disagreements.support: On Gaussian synthetics and noisy Ricker synthetics SCFS is less accurate than IFWE, which the authors attribute to its added synthetic parameters (Figures 6, 10).
disagreements.quote: The added parameters bring certain errors so that the accuracy of the SCFS method cannot reach that of the CFS method.

alternatives_considered.chosen: Replace the symmetry index with the standard deviations of the source and attenuated spectra
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Recalculating an optimal symmetry index by average or least-squares methods; the SCFS synthetic wavelet approach
alternatives_considered.reason: Parameters can be obtained directly from the spectrums without additional methods, and they vary with attenuation

alternatives_considered.chosen: Fix (n+1)f0 while varying n in the FWE illustration
alternatives_considered.reason: If f0 is fixed and n varies, the centre of the spectrum moves, making asymmetry changes hard to compare

alternatives_considered.chosen: Upper frequency limit of 90 Hz for the noise experiments
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Upper frequency limits from 120 to 40 Hz
alternatives_considered.reason: To show the detailed differences between them

alternatives_considered.chosen: Treat the field spectra as near-FWE and apply SCFS and IFWE
alternatives_considered.reason: The modelled FWE function matches the wavelet spectrums better than the other functions
